title: A 65-Year-Old's Heart Shifted Right After Meals, and Doctors Traced It to a Rare Diaphragm Anomaly
text:
A 65-Year-Old's Heart Shifted Right After Meals, and Doctors Traced It to a Rare Diaphragm Anomaly
When surgeons opened a 65-year-old man's chest for heart bypass surgery, they found his heart pushed far to the right. For two years, doctors blamed a missing lung lobe. The real explanation proved stranger: a weak, abnormally high diaphragm let his stomach and colon swell upward after meals, nudging his heart out of place before it slid back as his gut emptied.
Physicians at Alborz University of Medical Sciences in Karaj, Iran, reported the case on August 5, 2026, in Case Reports in Pulmonology. The authors say that, to their knowledge, it is the first report of this kind of reversible, meal-triggered heart shift in an adult with congenital diaphragmatic eventration.
A Heart Attack, Then a Puzzling Surgery
The man, a smoker who had a heart attack three years earlier, came to an emergency room with constant chest pain spreading to his left arm and jaw. Tests showed a type of heart attack known as NSTEMI, and an echocardiogram revealed that his heart was displaced and pumping somewhat weakly, with an ejection fraction of 45%. Angiography found disease in three coronary arteries, and bypass surgery was planned.
His exam was already unusual. Breath sounds were absent on the right side of his chest, and his heart sounds were heard toward the middle and left. Because the hospital's X-ray unit had failed, doctors went straight to CT, which showed an elevated left diaphragm, though the initial reading did not fully describe it.
During the operation, the surgeon noted severe rightward displacement of the heart and an overinflated left lung. The team attributed this to an underdeveloped or absent middle lobe of the right lung, an explanation that seemed confirmed when bronchoscopy after surgery appeared to show a missing airway branch. Breathing tests showed a moderately obstructive pattern.
A Second Look Two Years Later
The man returned two years later with a new complaint: heartburn after eating. Fresh imaging overturned the earlier conclusion. The right middle lobe was not missing after all; it was present but tucked into an unusual position toward the back of his chest.
The real problem sat beneath his left lung. Imaging showed congenital eventration of the left diaphragm, a condition in which part of the muscle never fully develops and is replaced by thin, fibrous tissue. Unlike a hernia, the diaphragm stays intact, but it sits abnormally high. His stomach and part of his colon had moved up into the space beneath it.
Ultrasound, fluoroscopy and dynamic MRI then captured the key finding. After meals, his distended stomach raised pressure inside his abdomen and pushed the colon upward, shifting his heart to the right. When his stomach and bowel emptied, the heart returned to its original position. On fluoroscopy, the shift exceeded normal breathing-related movement, which the authors say points to a true abnormality. The tests also ruled out diaphragm paralysis, which can look similar on still images.
Not Dextrocardia, but a Heart Being Pushed
The distinction matters. In dextrocardia, the heart is built to sit on the right from birth. In dextroposition, a normally formed heart is pushed or pulled rightward by something around it. On CT, his aorta sat in its normal position, which helped rule out dextrocardia.
Diaphragmatic eventration has fooled doctors before. A 2011 BMJ Case Reports image described a 70-year-old woman with pain after meals whose eventration had been misdiagnosed as dextrocardia. In the authors' review of adult cases, most involved the left side and the stomach or colon, and a 2014 report described a 70-year-old man with eventration and a heart fixed on the right side. Reports of a heart that moves back and forth with digestion are exceedingly limited, they wrote.
Symptoms tied to eating are not unusual in this condition. In a Chinese hospital's review of 26 adults treated for diaphragmatic eventration, 18 had chest discomfort after eating, and 25 of the 26 had the left side affected.
Scans also showed long-standing widening of his colon without any blockage. Blood tests for electrolytes, thyroid function, and inflammation were normal, and doctors judged the enlarged colon a chronic, incidental finding.
Medication Instead of Diaphragm Surgery
Severe eventration can be treated with plication, a procedure that folds and stitches the weakened diaphragm flat. Citing a National Library of Medicine review of diaphragm eventration, the authors note that adult guidance supports it for persistent shortness of breath, repeated lung infections, or worsening displacement of chest structures. He had none of those.
He was given a proton pump inhibitor for possible reflux and a laxative to keep his bowels moving. Doctors also advised him to quit smoking and avoid strenuous resistance exercise.
The authors suggested the meal-related shift could help explain his original chest pain. That link remains uncertain, since he also had a confirmed heart attack and severe coronary artery disease. The report describes one patient, does not specify exactly how far his heart moved, and offers no long-term follow-up after treatment.
Chest pain, especially pain that spreads to the arm or jaw, should always be treated as a possible emergency. People who notice chest discomfort, heartburn, or breathlessness that reliably follows meals should raise it with a doctor.
Key Questions Answered
What happened to the patient?
Imaging showed his heart shifted to the right after meals and returned to its original position as his stomach and bowel emptied.
What is diaphragmatic eventration?
It is a condition in which part of the diaphragm muscle is underdeveloped, leaving the diaphragm intact but abnormally high.
Why did his heart move?
The authors proposed that a distended stomach raised abdominal pressure and pushed his colon upward, displacing the heart.
Was he first misdiagnosed?
Yes. Doctors initially thought part of his right lung was missing, but later imaging showed the lobe was present in an unusual position.
How was he treated?
With reflux medication, a laxative, advice to quit smoking, and limits on strenuous resistance exercise. He did not have the problems that usually justify diaphragm surgery.
Did the heart shift cause his chest pain?
That is unclear. He also had a confirmed heart attack and disease in three coronary arteries.
